titulo: My Birthday's Bad Album Extravaganza Part XI: Odin this
texto:
There is something incredibly perverted about the westernization (or rather, the globalization) of Norse mythology and history that has been taking place the last two decades. Suddenly everyone who is able to grow facial hair on the internet is larping as a viking, arguing in various online forums that “Ummm actually, just because I live in Tucson, Arizona and my father is from Pakistan, I still have Viking blood in me!”. Needless to say, these are the type of people claiming to be experts on the subject, making claims that the northmen of the 9th century were everything that matches their current beliefs, and nothing like those of the current day wrongdoers. Now, as much as I’d like to keep going on a tangent about how these people are a blight on society, and how them LARPing is more annoying than your average genre-tourist-supremacist, I’m here to talk about the music of Brothers of Metal. A band whose sole purpose is to make the most superficial, generic, and whimsical pop metal so that the aforementioned group of halfwits can have music for their short form videos of them grooming their chest-hair or something.

First of all - despite the fact that I really want to call this a cheerful version of post 2006 Amon Amarth for those who hate growls - the band plays power metal. The kind of power metal that feels right at home in a Napalm Records or Nuclear Blast roster, extremely overproduced for the maximum mass appeal, which is further amplified by a handful of other focus group decisions we’ll get to. As such, the overall profile of the songs lacks any sort of grittiness, which the band tries desperately to make up for by forcing epic undertones under everything in a very unnatural, juvenile way that’s not unlike a Disney soundtrack. All is to say, I cannot take their efforts seriously, as every step of the way their sound conveys that stakes of their stories are negligible at best, missing that genuine and… intimate(?) feel epic heavy metal bands have. But if you’d like some power metal comparisons, BoM is lost somewhere between the boring overblown theatrics of Sabaton, the weaker riffless moments of (the significantly better) Orden Ogan, and any generic woman fronted band that lacks the songwriting talent. Speaking of which, there is another gimmick at play - other than the lyrical themes that is – and that would be how they needed 8 people to make shallow oven-fodder metal, while Sabaton and Gloryhammer can do it with 5 to 6 musicians.

With this small village behind each song, one must wonder if there is a good reason behind this decision or is it just the case of a local musical theatre troupe trying their hand at metal and not wanting to leave any of their friends out. Well, I can tell you right now that they barely have enough riffs for half a guitarist, let alone three of them. The occasional moment when they strike harmony – like they do in the intro of Kaunaz Dagaz - is nice, but most of the time it’s still repetitive marching riffs and rhythmic, non-groovy chugging, with the lead guitars rarely presenting anything worthwhile.  Now, there are songs with acoustic sections on them which are honestly very competent at setting the mood, and they feel refreshing after the piles of plastic power metal we just had to sit through. Issue is, said mood is extremely cliché and lame, making me roll my eye cringing instead of feeling any sort of excitement. 

We are going 60 OPM (Odins per minute) throughout the entire record, having to suffer through gems like Powersnake. What’s next? Valkyries of Destiny? Hammer of Strength? Rune of Victory? It sounds a lot more like a 5-year old’s drawing or a randomly generated D&D item than an actual song title, but I digress. It’s all warriors this, hammer that, and Odin, Odin, Odin, sometimes Thor if we are lucky. But as I don’t consider lyrics and the limited vocabulary of their writer to be part of my rating, let’s talk about the delivery that makes it all incredibly unlikable. Again, three people are listed as singers on this album, but in reality, it’s mostly just the duel between the soulless vocals of Ylva only Disney adults would find special, and one of the dudes delivering the generic dude-bro raspy Viking roleplaying vocals. Okay, I’m being very rude right now, but there are truly no other ways to describe how pointless and toothless it all feels. Had this come out couple years later than it did, I would have thought it was AI generated with how it hits every single power metal stereotype head-on to create shallowest possible record. Really, this is exactly what non-metalheads think is “cool” and “badass” and “metal”, and it sends shivers down my spine.

Objectively speaking, the members can sing, but there is only so much How To Train Your Dragon soundtrack worthy choruses I can listen to before I lose interest, and I’m afraid we get past that point by Weaver of Fate. Mind you, that’s only because the preceding Theft of the Hammer is actually the one non-acoustic song that I got zero complaints about (aside from the lyrics of course). It gets your blood pumping early on with an actual noteworthy, sharp lead section over the galloping rhythm guitars, then the vocals deliver great, harmonic melody that finally feels like there is true power and thought behind it. Its heftiness is nearly cut short with a bridge section that’s a tad bit out of place for my taste, but I won’t let it ruin the one song from the record I enjoy. Okay, enjoy is a strong word, because while there aren’t any glaring issues with the track, I’d consider it a filler on an above average power metal record. Talking about a heap of shit making a muddy puddle look good.

At the end of the day, Emblas Saga sits at 55 minutes in length, so for every minute I enjoy, there is 4-5 more that makes me roll my eyes. Best way to put what the record is like is that it’s extremely bland, store-brand vanilla ice cream made from budget ingredients, presented as a gourmet meal. The moment you look deeper than the surface with its shiny choruses and fancy production, you’ll find nothing but shortcomings, half-assed ideas, and very little things I could call charming. If you want to listen to genuine metal music themed around medieval Scandinavian heritage and such, you are far better off listening to Manegarm, Windir, or even Skálmöld, and leave this superficial marketing scheme to those with a funko pop collection.

Also: ODIN!

titulo: Concept album as it should be
texto:
Cradle Of Filth must have a soft spot for concept albums. Godspeed... is their second 100% concept album (after 1998’s Cruelty and a Beast), but Dani & Co. have often used a theme spanning a number of songs on other albums, as well. The album story is told in a traditional, chronological order and takes on the ghastly figure of Gilles de Rais, a XV century French knight who fought under Joan d’Arc against the English in the Hundred Years’ War and was even appointed a Marshal of France for his military bravery. Soon though (at the age of 30) de Rais retired from the military and public life altogether, pursuing his own interests and desires. Having accumulated massive wealth in the war, he soon squandered most of the money and desperately sought to regain the fortune. 

It was then when he turned to an Italian astrologer Francesco Prelati, who advised de Rais to seek help from a demon called Barron. Upon summoning Barron, de Rais sacrificed infants on a specially devised altar. De Rais’ accomplices kidnapped local peasants’ children, luring them into the woods surrounding Gilles’ property and dragging them in sacks into castle dungeons. Adolescent victims suffered numerous tortures, including sexual abuse before death. Total number of murdered children could not be exactly estimated, but amounts to hundreds. 

Gilles de Rais’ crimes were discovered by the clergy due to a series of circumstantial incidents. Soon a trial followed and the child molester and murderer was hanged, previously receiving pardon from the Church. Testimony of his crimes was kept secret for centuries and has been revealed not so long ago. 

During the decade preceding release of Godspeed On The Devil’s Thunder Cradle Of Filth transformed from an extreme gothic band with black metal influences into a gothic metal band. In short, they were becoming softer with every year and blatant use of inspiration from Iron Maiden (in guitar parts) didn’t help to strengthen the band’s position (at least on metal scene), either. The band (especially Dani and Paul – responsible for 100% of lyrical and musical ideas, respectively) sat in a circle, held hands, chanted motivational slogans and meditated how to return to the top. Soon they realized the witch had given John bad medicine... 

So is the music heavier? Sure as hell it is! Hiring Martin Skaroupka to replace Adrian Erlandsson behind the drum kit seems purposeful – there’s plenty of double bass and blastbeats going on and the new drummer proves he’s not getting paid for fucking around. It has to be noted that drums sound more powerful – stronger, thicker, with more bass sound – than on early Cradle Of Filth albums. Guitar-wise, I can only recall one instance of ripping off from Adrian Smith and Dave Murray, otherwise it’s pure Cradle of Filth in its unique and exquisite self. Vocally it is a strong performance from Dani, who diversifies range of expression as usual, although fans of early Cradle albums often complain that the (in)famous screeching is gone. Well...it is gone, like it or leave it, I’m staying! 

I don’t want to dwell on my view on highs and lows of this album. First of all, each listener might judge them differently – Cradle Of Filth is a very polarizing band, in the end. I also don’t think this album has any lows at all – if I were to throw out anything out of these 70+ minutes, it might have been half of one song, that’s it. Instead, I’m going to concentrate on some characteristic parts of the album.

After a keyboard introduction the album kicks of with “Shat Out Of Hell”, the album’s most fierce and fastest track, which is closest to what CoF used to play in ‘good old days’. It’s a simple song, but once it gets into your head, there is no way out! Two songs that follow may be regarded as most ‘poppy’ elements in de Rais puzzle. “The Death of Love” is built upon vocal dialogue between Dani and a female voice, while “The 13th Caesar”...is more or less the same, although stronger and catchier, with a great chorus, with awesome combination of choir, female and male vocals. Note that neither of these two tracks, seemingly softer than the rest,  was chosen to promote the album. 

The video was shot for “Honey and Sulphur”, a majestic song which, story-wise, introduces the black magic element in the story of Gilles de Rais. The solemn choir part, chanting a Latin proverb (Praeclarum Custodem Ovium Lupum which translates into Wayne Rooney’s native tongue as An excellent protector of sheep – the wolf), set against brutal vocals and a thoroughly fast and heavy song guarantees creeps all over the body, especially when witnessed live. As far as speed and brutality goes, there are two more killer songs: “Darkness Incarnate” (with spoken introduction from Dani’s daughter Luna) and the title track. Especially blastbeats in the first one are worth a headbang or two. But it doesn’t mean that other songs are soft or slow. There’s a lot going on in them: e.g. “Sweetest Maleficia” is really crazy rhythm-wise, while “Midnight Shadows Crawl to Darken Counsel with Life” has weird bridges were all instruments go silent, there’s only a very fast high-pitched keyboard playing in the background (like in culminating moments of old horror flicks) and Dani’s half-shriek half-whisper. “Ten Leagues Beneath Contempt” is a mid-paced creepy crawler with excellent and very tight rhythmic section which creates excellent groove. Overall, if you ever liked any Cradle Of Filth, this album won’t leave you bored.

The story is told mainly through lyrics, which are sang in 98% by Dani, minus some female vocals in “The Death of Love” and “The 13th Caesar”. Many songs include spoken introductions from Doug Bradley (actor famous for the role of Pinhead in Hellraiser series) and boy, they are a pleasure to listen to! Bradley’s voice, meant to utter Gilles’ own words, instantly sets the atmosphere for the song in the right tone. 

Have you ever been into Cradle Of Filth’s music? Do you like King Diamond concept albums, but would like the stories to be less cheesy and the music heavier? Do you enjoy blastbeats AND catchy melodies on one album? If you answered ‘yes’ to any of these questions, then make yourself a favor and grab this album, preferably in the limited edition, with some cool extra tracks, including a cover of Celtic Frost’s “Into the Crypt of Rays” (which also deals with evil deeds of the infamous Marshal of France).

My first listen through this album, I couldn't help but feel pure excitement that the album sounded as good as it did. From the first few seconds, I knew this felt like Northland. The very folk-focused instrumentation and ambient natural sounds make a beautiful introduction to the album's tone and message, and instantly get you in the mood. Right from the start, the music sounds like a very refined and polished version of their first album, with much more focus and direction. The production value is noticeably higher, not necessarily in the quality of the recording, but in the mixing and the fine tuning of each individual instrument and sound. 

	The guitars are just as good as always, with even more focus on matching the melodies to those of the flutes and strings. But it never gets too overpowered by these, and is constantly setting the pace, often mimicking a horse gallop. The drumming feels much more precise and progressive, which is a welcomed change in the typical folk metal scene. It is not overpowering, but not underwhelming, and sits at just the right place. Even the use of synth and folk instruments has been improved on, which is hard to believe considering their prominence on the previous album. They feel natural, unforced, and completely believable.

	Lyrically, the album has a pretty interesting story. To make things brief, it talks about how humanity has failed the natural world and needs to be wiped out and restarted. While it sounds like a very corny and cliche theme, it actually works very well with the Northland sound, especially considering they have folk instruments and natural ambient sounds that are more prominent than the guitars at times. While listening to the lyrics, you are fully transported to the world that the album creates, and you can fully feel the message behind each line. The incredible vocal work plays a huge role in this.

	In the previous album, the vocal style was quite varied, but in this one, that variation is increased massively and done in a much more musically tasteful way. My main issue with the previous was the clean vocals, which sounded very off. It is clear that they have had some practice since then, because the clean vocals in this album are some of the best in all of folk metal. From death metal styled grunting, black metal screams, and folk metal chanting, this album features it all. At one point, only clean vocals and acoustic instruments are used, swapping between male and female vocals. It leaves a beautiful break during the climax of the action that sounds like something Howard Shore would write. This vocal dexterity is what honestly sets the album apart from other folk metal releases of the last few years. 

	To sum it all up, this album is exactly the album that it should have been; and more. I went into it blindly, not sure what to expect. The previous album was great, but felt slightly off, so I was hoping this one would fix that. Boy, did it ever. It completely flipped my expectations and instantly became one of my favorite albums of the year, perhaps even the last five. If you liked the first album, you will love this. If you like heartfelt and genuine folk metal, you will love this. Even people who hate this sub-genre will likely be able to enjoy what  Downfall and Rebirth  has to offer. If this band doesn't hit the big time and become the next Ensiferum after this one, I won't know what to think, because this was one hell of a joy ride.

It was a whole different world out there when Saxon released their first LP, way back in 1979 (yeah, "when the dam began to burst" and whatever). Many things we now take for granted simply weren't there yet, such as internet, global warming, cellphones, digital music and NWOBHM, to name a few. That said, it's just natural that Biff Byford (V), Paul Quinn (G), Graham Oliver (G), Steve Dawson (B), and Pete Gill (D) still didn't know exactly what to do with their music and it should come as no surprise to learn that it shows on Saxon's eponymous debut album, though was far from ruining it, fortunately.

It all begins with "Rainbow Theme / Frozen Rainbow", an epic heavy ballad slightly in a Uriah Heep vein and with more than a hint of prog rock in it. A good start, but not very representative if we're to be strict here. Then the band delivers "Big Teaser", a tune with a glam rock feel which strongly reminds me of Marc Bolan. And then side one comes to an ending with "Judgement Day", a competent (but kinda confused) attempt to write a convoluted song about the end of the world (c'mon, all metal bands have been there and done that). That means the whole A side of Saxon's debut LP presents no hints of their signature hard-hitting-metal-with-biker-themes attack, and that is to say something about how unsure of themselves the band seemed to be at this point.

Fortunately, side two comes to the rescue with the excellent "Stallions of the Highway" making a clear statement that an exciting new era in metal was just around the corner (or at the flip of an LP if you want to stretch the metaphor further). "Backs to the Wall" is also great in the same no-frills-heavy-metal fashion of the preceding tune, and I think that "Militia Guard" is a nice way to close proceedings, a creative number with a semi-acoustic epic feel and some nice twists and turns here and there. "Still Fit to Boogie" is, ahem, a boogie number without many redeeming factors, but it's reasonably funny and there's nothing fundamentally wrong about being funny, right?

The production is not good at all (most of all, it lacks punch and energy), but I guess the lackluster results of this studio visit paved the way for the heaviness to come, so it kinda was a good thing in the end. BTW, I guess the same can be said about the LP as a whole; it shows not only a band in search of its own musical personality, but also portrays a whole metal generation trying to take the '70s heritage one step further, but not yet sure how it should be done. Musically speaking, this is one for Saxon's (and NWOBHM's) hardcore fans, but those who fit the description will find a fair amount of songs to enjoy here. And if you're interested in the development of heavy metal through the years, then I'll also suggest you to give this one a spin or two.

titulo: A competent effort that needs more inspiration
texto:
Although this hour-long album consists of eight tracks, it plays more or less like one long continuous work with breaks and so I'm reviewing it as though it were. The whole album flows in a way that makes it seem like one major opus of several movements. The music ranges from psychedelic stoner doom metal with spacey and spaced-out effects to a tougher hardcore style and outbreaks of melodic lead guitar soloing, all layered with thick gritty or crunching guitar riffs and sub bass growl. The music is not too thick though and is clean in execution and production so the sound is very clear and plenty of space can be heard within songs: all this makes for a good listening experience where you can hear everything no matter how quiet or distant in the mix the vocals may be (and some spoken voice field recordings are very far back in the mix) and the music doesn't sound at all chaotic or murky.

The songs are well executed without being very outstanding: the Ufomammut guys don't quite come across as very inspired by the music and I have a sense of them being well-disciplined, a bit too much so for their own good and for the kind of music they play. I always think stoner and doom metal should be loose and a bit deranged, given its roots in the psychedelic and space rock of the past. If an album seems well-behaved, I always hope there'll be at least one track, even if a short instrumental one tagging as a bonus, where the musicians can simply let fly with a loose improvised jam. Anyway, two early tracks are very gritty, tough and aggressive but as the album progresses it starts to sound a bit pretentious and unconvincing, the middle track "Ammonia" being a case in point: mostly instrumental and meant to be a mini-opera of space fantasy, it sits oddly with the hard-edged aggressive songs around it. Of these more menacing, bared-teeth tracks, "Destroyer" is the best if short compared to the others, combining screaming vocals, militaristic riffs and a varied beat, with plenty of atmospheric slurpy space ambient tones in the background.

At over 21 minutes in length, "Void" is the axis around which "Idolum" revolves. At first I thought that this was the Ufomammut I've been waiting for the whole time while listening to "Idolum": thick lava-like sludge doom with a churning motorcycle undercoat of grind and crashing percussion. Perhaps the vocals could be a lot better - clearer in the mix, less screechy and haranguing, more like singing - but at least they don't detract from the instrumentation. Suddenly the track collapses into silence and I'm thinking "What the ....?" only to hear the piece build up slowly, imperceptibly almost. In this respect "Void" turns out to be a disappointment as this slow crawl, completely ambient and minimalist in style, takes up most of the track's running time. Fortunately the final track arrives with a huge bludgeoning guitar crash to save what's left of the album (not much).

There is some good aggressive music on the album but it's undermined by a lack of distinctive riffing on most tracks and a long track that delivers much less than listeners would expect of it, given the genre of music it sits within on the album. While experimenting with structure and genre is a laudable effort, it can also be a hazardous risk if not thought out or executed with regard for the limits and demands of the album's concept and the kind of music experience listeners expect from it. Because "Void" comes as the second-last track on "Idolum", clocking in at over 20 minutes, and because the album's genre of music is stoner doom with psychedelic and aggressive hardcore influences, the kind of experimentalism the band can afford would also have to satisfy listeners' expectations for something that justifies the build-up of previous songs (not that there is much), so while the slow minimalism is fine, it also needs to change into something that matches and balances the song's explosive beginning and that just didn't happen. 

"Idolum" is a competent album overall but I feel Ufomammut have the creative and technical potential to be great and they just need something extra to push them into more stratospheric levels.

During the later 90s when my Metallica worshipping days were coming to a slow end, I began seeking better music to mold my guitar and bass playing (at the time I was playing bass in an all Metallica cover band).  A lot of the better stuff I got I had to import from Japan, particularly this re-release of an old Helloween classic from part one of the Keeper series and the single for the up and coming new album “Better than Raw”.

Future World is obviously one of the happier songs that Kai Hansen put together during his tenure with the band, featuring a simple chord progression with a simple signature riff, not all that different from his more angst driven anthem “I want out”, though with a brief filling display at the end to close out what is quite a catchy song.

The new version of “Starlight” is vocally an improvement over its original incarnation with Kai doing the vocals, mostly because Kai voice was not quite as powerful and mature as it is on his Gamma Ray material.  Michael Kiske definitely gave the band its mainstream appeal with his cleaner yet still eccentric/quasi operatic vocal style.  The different version of “A Little Time” is a bit shorter, but still the same melodic anthem featuring a short solo interchange and an infectiously catchy chorus.

Japanese re-releases of old Helloween material are a godsend for Power Metal freaks like me because they always have plenty of additional perks.  If you liked the sound of the Keeper albums and want to hear what a classic Kai Hansen era song sounds like with different vocals, it would definitely be worth it to track this single down.

Here’s Grey Wolf’s Glorious Death, this Brazilian band’s third full-length album and my introduction to their work. On this album, they play a brand or rather unoriginal epic heavy metal that truly falls into the stereotype of “bland, second-rate heavy metal with barely a sliver of originality”. I hate to put it so bluntly, but it really is at the bottom of the barrel when it comes to the niche genre of modern traditional heavy metal, which is already a tough nut to crack if you’re looking for the goods. Fabio (lol) “Grey Wolf” (LOL) Paulinelli is the leading songwriter here, and he also provides lead vocals as well as bass guitar, so let us dig into the third opus of his  brainchild.

The core of the music on this record relies on two main things: the vocals and the riffs. Simple enough, right? Well, those elements may be pieces of the puzzle, but this album leaves their puzzle a good ways away from finished. It also seems like they spilled their beer, or whatever Brazilians drink, all over the puzzle too. All of the songs rely on that clichéd structure of a few verses and chorus’ with maybe a breakout riff section at the end or a softer, “we swear we weren’t trying to rip off the ‘Rime of the Ancient Mariner’ interlude” part, but nothing else. There are barely any solos, the riffs themselves are far too uninspired to leave a lasting impression, and the vocal melodies are so predictable that you almost know them before they show up. In addition to this, Fabio’s vocals on their own are horrible; they’re coarse and rough while simultaneously missing any passion whatsoever. As a whole, the album tries to rely on vocal melodies that don’t really work, riffs that have no meat on their bones, and songwriting that just does not make the cut. 

When it comes to positives, Glorious Death has a few, but they’re all too small and insignificant to save the weak songwriting at play; there are too many holes and not enough patches to fix them. But still, the album has only one terribly annoying song, that being “Cimmeria”, as well as a few energetic breakout riffs and decent bass playing to keep things from stagnating too horribly. Fabio’s bass playing is more than adequate, and he really helps to add some structural integrity to an otherwise frail framework. His fills are a bit too predictable, but he honestly out-performs the guitars in every respect, making for a bass-centric metal record, if that should be your fancy. Also, despite the drums being programmed, they don’t sound out of place at all, only a bit technically lacking (as programmed drums tend to be). So really, this album could have been an absolute nightmare, but it comes out at least somewhat enjoyable due to some neat bass work, a few admittedly decent riffs, and solid (if not too thin) production. 

In the end though, Glorious Death just fails. It's one of the least memorable things I've ever heard. The songs are short, yet they seem to drag on for too long (ouch, how do you screw up short songs?), the riffing lacks gusto, the vocals are just bad, and as a whole the album trips and falls into its own blade. Far from a glorious death of any kind, really. I guess I could recommend this to those who seriously cannot stop listening to modern traditional/epic heavy metal, but still, even for that crowd, this does not make the cut. I can't seriously recommend this to anybody. If you're a NWOTHM hunter, this is some weak game that ain't worth the trouble.

titulo: Don't be fooled by the name..
texto:
I came across this band only today when I saw they contributed to the soundtrack of possibly the greatest metal documentary ever made, Get Thrashed (See this. If you have not then as Paul Baloff says,” DIE”). Not that I hadn’t seen the documentary earlier it was the first time I really paid attention to the music played in the background and boy did it slay.

I came to know about the band through the Get Thrashed My Space page and ran over here to MA to get all details possible. Seeing this EP I got my hands on it as soon as possible and it does not disappoint.

Don’t be fooled by the rather lame EP name, Dudes of Darkness (Dudes!!? WTF!!!?), Because man does this consist some of the best modern day thrash material available today. The band contributed 2 tracks, Can U not Talk and The Law – Anthem to the aforesaid documentary. Both of these tracks are not surprisingly the best ones here.

The leads are something expected off of a 80’s thrash band in full flow. A shred fest, this EP contains a ton of riffs and the occasional, in your face, and face melting solo. The vocals are not the usual thrash type, but similar to that of Joey Belladona of Anthrax fame, Tobias Jansson reaches those high notes with no effort what so ever. The drums are a great here too. Aggressive, not hogging the limelight and a great talent is Johan Rudberg the drummer. The bass playing consists mainly of playing along with the guitar but once in a while comes in the bass slap and boy it’s heard.

The production is pretty awesome and it’s too hard to believe that it’s self-produced. Fuck record labels they say, let’s produce our own stuff and let us make it sound way better is their motto it seems.

So, if you yearn for underground, heavy as fuck old school thrash metal, then start hunting for this EP. It is one of te very few good thrash bands today.

For those curious about the Japanese sludge doom metal band Corrupted but who were put off listening to their albums because they'd heard that essential recordings like "Llenandose de Gusanos" and "El Mundo Frio" were very, very long and had the nature of endurance tests, you need not fear: throughout their career Corrupted released several EPs of manageable length. some of them less than 20 minutes in length. One day these EPs should all be gathered up and released on the one compilation album, that would be good for those people who aren't able to buy the music separately but can get it if it were all together in one product. "La victima es tu mismo" could qualify as singles material as its A-side is the title track and the B-side is a shorter song, less than half the length of the title track. The whole thing runs to just under 19 minutes.

As the shorter track, "Los Colores del Cielo" might be minor but it's still grand: noisy, oily guitars like pouring metallic rain and slightly floppy yet hard percussion accompany Hevi's gruff ranting. The music initially is no more than backdrop for the vocals but after the second minute the guitars start piling on the pressure and listeners feel the tension increase almost imperceptibly but steadily. The drums continue to lumber on as before. The continuous run of guitars, almost throbbing though actually not, has a deranged edge after some time. While I would have liked something dramatic and explosive to end the track, going out in a pyrotechnics display isn't Corrupted's style and the track leaves me feeling strung up high and struggling to come back down. I suspect I'll just have to cut loose and plummet down.

The title piece is slightly more varied and has at least definite though very slow and miasma-like rhythms and chugging riffs. It's more like a song than most other Corrupted pieces I've heard, with alternations between instrumental passages where effects and melodies may play and parts where Hevi croaks out lyrics, during which the music merely keeps time and rhythm. The instrumental parts sometimes feature very prolonged, high-pitched guitar feedback squeals set far back in the mix. After some time, the shrill parts dominate the track before fading out. Later the song changes to a more flowing and noisy metal shower with steady if perhaps monotonous drumming. Hevi's voice rarely changes from near-animalistic groaning and growling while the music becomes frantic and quite edgy and frazzled. Again, I find the ending not to my taste: I always feel with something this intense, suggestive of anger on the edge of explosion, that there's got to be some kind of release and resolution, even if not a very good one or one that satisfies most listeners.

The music is very much what Corrupted usually delivers: hard-hitting, no-frills sludge doom metal with plenty of crust and a pessimistic view of human frailty and corrupt politics and culture. These guys don't perform songs that most people would recognise as songs; Corrupted's songs are more like poetry readings or long declamations that happen to have a doom metal backing and an angry attitude born perhaps of idealism and yearning for a better world turned into despair and cynicism over the extent and depths of human depravity and corruption. The cover artwork of a silhouetted person looking out over a bleak and ruined urban landscape suggests something of that outlook.

Brought to me by a trusted friend, California's Voidhämmer gives a sensation of anything but the warm California sun. Swinging into the new year with their first and only release, Noxious Emissions is one of those 4-track death metal EPs that quickly eludes to a promising future. While not much to go off of yet, the band secures their ability to write crushing, murky rhythms under a fierce umbrella with thick gutturals to match the even thicker sludge of the atmosphere. The drums especially stand out, working double-time to ensure crushing blasts that grab the listener while also coating the bottom layer in thick muck to match everything else.

Diving into the filth factor right away, "Rotting In Excrement" wastes no time getting to the point, even laying down some almost technical chops amidst the more straightforward yet marshy rhythms. "Cadaveric Bloat" more or less follows suit, leading into "Phosphatized," probably my favorite track due to the punkish vibes let in by an even sharper guitar tone. If that isn't enough, the bass on this one stomps everything in its trail, before screeching into the closing "Coffin Leakage," smothering the listener with tough stomps.

Obviously Voidhämmer are still in their infancy, but if Noxious Emissions is anything to go off of, it's a pretty safe bet that they're capable of crafting a fucking stellar full-length. Do not sleep on this.

titulo: Joe Stump likes to shred. A lot.
texto:
Symphonic power metal is definitely a hit or miss type subject with me, either it's really overly symphonic and not the good type of symphonic, trading less metal elements and becoming more of a Within Temptation type band instead of utilizing symphonic elements, being grandiose and epic all while still remaining a metal band. HolyHell is one such band that seems to understand this, although it's not quite as consistent as it should be, on their first single Apocalypse containing 4 choice songs displaying quite a professional approach to the genre, probably owing much debt to master shredder Joe Stump and his knowledge of the music business and such. 

The first song, the title song, being the best here featuring awesome symphonic type orchestrations allowing for a very grandiose and majestic feel feeling like something from Luca Turilli's side projects meets neo-classical bliss in this fast number that creates quite the imagery. I can clearly see myself standing on the ramparts of a castle whilst arrows darken the sky and legions of foot soldiers clashing on the fields below, bloody and guts everywhere and maybe a fucking Nazgul flying at me, especially at the 1 minute mark; yeah... you know what I'm talking about.

What makes this a bit more unique is the lead vocals of Maria Breon and her Simone Simons like approach, but probably not quite in the same league as her. Breon's still very talented and knows how to sing, she's nowhere as operatic as her colleagues but still knows what she's doing. The drums are what you should expect to find here with double bass euphoria and guitar riffs mixed perfectly with keyboards that scream neo-classical symphonies, being very similar to that of Rhapsody.

Resurrection is more of your stereotypical symphonic power metal song with some gothic metal type riffing and drumming patterns. It's not as powerful and doesn't strike as well as the title track, but the lead guitar work is fantastic and being a slower ballad-esque type song, it highlights Breon's vocals very well, showcasing her range very well. Mixing lower type slow singing to rapid fast falsettoes almost, doing a very good job. Last Vision is similar in this aspect, though once again featuring very nice symphonic elements but lacking the powerful punch that Apocalypse had; this once again showcases a slower and more traditional symphonic power metal song approach. 

Out of nowhere these is a live song from the Masters of Rock Festival in 2005 being a cover of the infamous Phantom of the Opera, which every symphonic metal band does, but being slightly more unique featuring the one and only legend himself, Eric Adams. I've always enjoyed this song, especially Nightwish's rendition of it and HolyHell's cover is quite decent getting the crowd into it and making it more energetic. Breon does a good job, as she should because she's quite talented and Eric Adams, being the metal vocalist god that he is does a very good job, but unfortunately it doesn't do as well because there are no orgasmic ridiculous falsettoes that I wish for every night... fortunately though the mighty Joe Stump makes up for it shredding and soloing all over the place making it much more. At the end though, when the crowd is going nuts as Stump shreds the fuck out of the guitar and Breon does her best Tarja impression, Adams should have been ripping out one of his infamous "Kingdom Come" ending falsettoes, oh well, I suppose he didn't want to steal HolyHell's thunder.

So HolyHell does a decent job with this first release/single and has quite the professional touch with this, with Joe Stump's help and influence in the band making it a lot better that it would be and more unique. It's absolutely nothing out of the ordinary, but it's quite unique in it's own right making it a decent offering. This is worth picking up just for the title track alone, it being such a fantastic symphonic power metal song that packs quite a punch and has such majestic orchestrations. Fans of Rhapsody, Luca Turilli, symphonic power metal as well as shredders take note and watch out for HolyHell's upcoming full-length.

This is the beginning of Primordial, one of the most talented bands of all time. This demo is over 22 minutes long with immaculate production; every instrument can be easily heard. 

The music is really heavy & not insanely fast as most of the black metal bands, Primordial was different from the start, this is different black metal, the bass is really prominent, some parts of the song heavily consist of bass, the music is catchy and groovy to an extent because of the bass. The vocals are typical black metal shrieks full of intensity. There are some doom metal elements here but not as much as in their future releases, just as you think that what else can be here then the clean vocals appear for a while in few of the songs & there’s a little guitar solo in “The Darkest Flame” as well but it stays in the background. The guitar riffs are interesting as they’re not standard black metal riffs as well as the drumming because it sometimes become catchy but most of time it’s average extreme metal drumming. Vocals are mostly harsh but are decipherable, the lyrics however are interesting, and they are about paganism, romance, depression & nature. Overall these four songs can easily be cherished by not only black metal fans but also by fans of suicidal, black doom & heavy metal fans. There are no celtic / folk elements in this demo whatsoever. 

This is a good effort but their later albums are far superior to this demo.

Man, where to even start with this one? Sun Eater, the lesser of two death metal-related albums to bear that title in 2014, and Job for a Cowboy's fourth full-length, is an exercise in variation and ability which at the very least sounds like it required a lot of effort in both its conception and execution. The question is, whether or not that was all worth it? My answer is very, very nearly. This is not a band that I'd ever accuse of having a 'personality', despite the quirky name, which many have already ranted over but at least isn't just another -tion, -tory, for you to file away under redundant. Once they shifted away from their insipid meathead deathcore roots into a more decidedly West Coast approximation of modern, semi-tech death which traced its lineage to all the 'right' acts in the field (Suffocation, Morbid Angel, Deicide and Cannibal Corpse could all be heard in the controlled chaos), they seemed to translate into a more respectable, though still highly divisive act. I've enjoyed a few of their efforts (Demonocracy, Genesis, etc) to an extent, but greatness has ever eluded the Arizona quartet, and despite a very painstakingly wrought effort here, it still does...

Much like Fallujah transformed into a modern approximation of classic Cynic, with whirlwind technicality alternated against a more ambient/jazzy fusion, Job for a Cowboy have done the next best thing and decided to channel Atheist. Alright, not exactly, but a number of times I was sitting through this I kept getting Unquestionable Presence impressions, with some of the cleaner guitar patterns reminiscent also of Gorguts' Obscura. This is an acrobatic, eccentric slab of technical death and thrash metal which goes to great lengths to try and distinguish itself from its aesthetic ancestors, applying a modern studio context to their now antiquated, but once innovative ideas. But like so many other young death metal bands with athletic instrumental skill, it seems to rely a little too much on its own frenetic diversity and not on the strong songwriting chops that will make or break a death metal record throughout eternity. I'm not saying Sun Eater is void of a few gorgeous lead sequences, or riffs that perk my interest, but where The Flesh Prevails became this largely consistent pendulum of ethereal melodies and butchering brutality, this one just never develops much of an identity beyond the 'hey, wow, listen to that' mentality, where you're temporarily blown away by a band's proficiency set and not at any risk of remembering what they are actually setting down.

Oh, don't get me wrong, this one is compelling...to an extent. Jonny Davy's gruesome snarls and growls are splattered all over the polished, punchy instrumentation like cattle organs in some spit-shined slaughterhouse whose death machines are fresh off the assembly line. But did I like them? Nah, they try really hard but accomplish little since he just can't contort them into interesting syllabic patterns. Danny Walker's guest drumming on this is technically brilliant but I found a few of the components like the snares and toms to feel a little too Tupperware at points. The bass is amazing in general, with lines highly similar to those used in prog thrash and prog death classics like Control and Resistance, Unquestionable Presence, Focus, etc, and there are parts of the album where I really felt like I could just listen to Nick Schendzielos isolated from the rest of the band and be happy. But at the same time, it's actually the Glassman/Sannicandro guitar duo which keeps the busiest, and offers us the most contrast and variation between the different levels of distorted excess. The album boasts a Jason Suecof production with Eyal Levi and several other engineers, so you know it's going to have that pristine, clinical 21st century death metal gloss that most of the 'forward thinking' acts strive towards, but then again that's just not anything new at this point.

Effort was extended towards the lyrics, also, but they end up the sort that feel like they're waxing all philosophical about the digital age, moral relativity; poetic and neatly scrawled imagery, sure, but for some reason it felt like a bunch of fancy words strung together which are ultimately as meaningless as taking a hearty poop. But I guess I could say that about almost any death metal band that dares transcend the serial killings, gore menageries and so forth. Job for a Cowboy tried, it's just such a fine line between an actual message of substance and mere pretentious twaddle. I felt like these were keeping one foot on either side of that line. And that's sort of symptomatic of Sun Eater in general: a Herculean attempt to progress and expand one further circumference beyond the burly BroStep brutality of the band's origins than even their last few albums dared. Nothing to scoff at, since tunes like "Buried Monuments" rank among their better compositions, but ultimately I just felt hollow after a few spins, like I was watching some flashy action movie which had a couple impressive stunts but no quotable one-liners like Commando or Terminator. This is more like the last four Jason Statham flicks you caught. Huge, kinetic, smarmy, lots of explosions and special effects, but more of a rental than a purchase. 

-autothrall
